title: SECURE Grid Act
official_title: To amend the Energy Policy and Conservation Act to require States to include supporting the physical security, cybersecurity, and resilience of local distribution systems in State energy security plans.
likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Robert E. Latta (R-OH) and passed the House by voice vote (no recorded roll call); the bill folds local-distribution-system security into existing State energy security plans and now awaits Senate consideration.
summary: Updates the federal law on State energy security plans so States also plan for the physical security, cybersecurity, and resilience of local electric distribution systems — the lower-voltage lines and equipment that deliver power to communities. It adds these systems and their equipment suppliers to what State plans must address.
brief: Requires State energy security plans to address the security and resilience of local electric distribution systems.

top_lines.headline: Local Distribution Systems in State Plans
subs: Defines a local distribution system as utility energy infrastructure at 100 kilovolts or less
State plans must address physical attacks on local distribution and the bulk-power system
State plans must address cybersecurity threats that may impact the bulk-power system

top_lines.headline: Equipment Suppliers and Supply Chain
subs: Adds suppliers of electricity generation, transmission, and distribution equipment to consultation
State plans must address supply chain risks for that equipment
Plans must address weather-related threats and vulnerabilities

top_lines.headline: State Determination and Timeline
subs: A State plan submission is not required to be approved by the Secretary
Statutory year reference in subsection (i) changed from 2025 to 2030
Adds a risk mitigation approach for reliability and end-use resilience

items.main: Names the Act the "Securing Community Upgrades for a Resilient Grid Act" or the "SECURE Grid Act".
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Consideration of the Security of Local Distribution Systems in State Energy Security Plans

items.main: Amends Section 366 of the Energy Policy and Conservation Act (42 U.S.C. 6326) to add "local distribution system," defined as any energy infrastructure owned and operated by an electric utility at a voltage of 100 kilovolts or less.
items.detail: The new definition is added to subsection (a). Subsection (h) is also amended to insert "local distribution system" after "electric utility," extending existing plan provisions to cover these systems.

items.main: Rewrites the hazards a State plan must address to include physical threats, physical attacks on local distribution systems and the bulk-power system, supply chain risks for electricity equipment, and cybersecurity threats to local distribution systems that may impact the bulk-power system.
items.detail: Subsection (c)(3) is replaced to list weather-related threats, physical attacks, and supply chain risks as physical threats, plus a separate cybersecurity category. Subsection (c)(5) is replaced to require a risk mitigation approach to enhance reliability and end-use resilience, including responding to, mitigating, and recovering from those hazards.

items.main: Adds suppliers of electricity generation, transmission, and distribution equipment to the parties States consult (subsection (b)(2)); adds suppliers of generation and transmission equipment to the coordination provision (subsection (d)(3)); and lets States submit plans without the Secretary’s approval.
items.detail: Subsection (b)(2) and subsection (d)(3) are amended to add equipment suppliers. Subsection (e) is restructured to state that a plan submission is not required to be approved by the Secretary. Subsection (i) is amended by striking "2025" and inserting "2030."

underreported.summary: A State plan submission is not required to be approved by the Secretary; States self-determine the content submitted.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill expands what plans must address, but this provision establishes that the Secretary does not approve the submission, leaving plan sufficiency to the State rather than federal review.

underreported.summary: The provision striking "2025" and inserting "2030" changes the year referenced in subsection (i) of the amended statute.
underreported.why_unreported: The date change is a single-word amendment separate from the bill headline on security and resilience, adjusting the timeframe in the underlying statute.

gaps: The bill requires plans to address cybersecurity threats to local distribution systems but does not specify security standards, funding, or penalties for those systems.
The bill adds equipment suppliers to consultation but does not define which suppliers qualify or address foreign-sourced equipment beyond a general supply chain risk category.
The bill states a plan submission need not be approved by the Secretary but does not describe any federal review or consequence if a plan omits the newly required hazards.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Latta
featured_quotes.text: State energy security plans, or SESPs, provide States with an opportunity to identify threats and vulnerabilities in their respective energy networks. This collaborative process ensures that States can stay on the cutting edge of an evolving threat landscape. While the initial exercise of SESPs has meaningfully assisted States in managing their energy systems, there is room for improvement to enhance visibility and threat detection and to holistically consider disparate vulnerabilities across the sector.

added: New statutory definition of "local distribution system" as utility energy infrastructure at 100 kilovolts or less
New requirement that State plans address physical attacks and supply chain risks for electricity equipment, and cybersecurity threats to local distribution systems
New provision that a State plan submission is not required to be approved by the Secretary
modified: Amends Section 366 of the Energy Policy and Conservation Act (42 U.S.C. 6326) to add equipment suppliers to consultation and to rewrite the hazards and risk mitigation paragraphs
Changes the year reference in subsection (i) from 2025 to 2030
